episode_thesis: Yoav Git reads three papers through a trend follower's lens. The inelastic markets hypothesis ($1 of inflow lifts US equity valuation about $5) is useful because elasticity and adjustment speed set how big and how long trends are, but its 5x multiplier is probably nearer 1 because trend-following flows are a reverse-causality channel. The Man AHL inflation paper shows trend (commodity and fixed income) works in inflationary periods and suits inflation-linked mandates better than TIPS or real estate, and the backtest-overfitting paper shows alternative-beta (QIS) products lose about 60% of their backtest Sharpe live, so portfolio construction, risk management and execution matter more than the signal.

speakers.name: Yoav Git
speakers.role: CTA manager (London; trades illiquid/niche markets with about 25% correlation to the liquid trend universe; formerly at Man)
speakers.speaker_note: Name is a caption spelling (Yove/Yo). Alan Dunne guest-hosts (Niels is away). Two-speaker conversation; attribution is clear from content. Ledger corrections applied: C05-1 (a price-impact multiplier, not an elasticity) and C06-2 (the transcript is garbled: 0.2% or 2%).

worldview_premises.premise: Trend size depends on the elasticity of supply and demand: inelastic markets (electricity, commodities) need a large price move to clear a shock, and delayed adjustment (cows take a year to grow) makes the trend persist.
worldview_premises.support: Supply-demand explanation with butter, cows and electricity examples

worldview_premises.premise: Elasticities are hard to estimate because shocks hit both curves; an instrument that moves only one side is needed, and the Gabaix-Koijen granular instrumental variable uses shifts in each holder's share of demand as idiosyncratic shocks.
worldview_premises.support: Explains the method and has corresponded with the authors

worldview_premises.premise: In the inelastic markets hypothesis $1 of inflow into US equities raises aggregate valuation by about $5, so flows drive valuations (a possible bubble) and the efficient market view fails.
worldview_premises.support: Reports the paper's result (Gabaix and Koijen), not his own estimate

worldview_premises.premise: Fixed income reacts far less to flows than equities: $1 trillion of Fed buying in the GFC did not lift bond prices by 50%, because Treasury supply expands to meet demand while equity supply (about $500bn of issuance a year) is tied to the real economy.
worldview_premises.support: QE natural experiments and US Treasury growth from $10tn to $25tn (ledger-corrected: price-impact multiplier of 0.25-0.75 versus 5)

worldview_premises.premise: The paper's contemporaneous regression confuses causality: rising equity prices attract trend-following flows (CTAs, closet trend followers, funds, retail), so the true flow-impact multiple is probably just above 1.
worldview_premises.support: Back-of-envelope: about $300bn of CTAs gives quarterly trend flows of roughly 0.2% or 2% of market value (garbled) against the 6% flow figure; no estimate of his own

worldview_premises.premise: The paper's data are slow and short (quarterly flow of funds, Morningstar fund flows and 13F, roughly 2000-2021), so only one quarter's horizon is shown and the multiplier cannot be tracked over time.
worldview_premises.support: Reading the paper's data description

worldview_premises.premise: Markets differ in how fast they adjust: equities find a new equilibrium quickly (ETF shares outstanding show strong weekly negative autocorrelation), whereas commodity prices become negatively autocorrelated only about a year out because supply takes a year to respond; more elastic markets have lower volatility (bonds versus equities).
worldview_premises.support: ETF shares-outstanding autocorrelation; physical supply constraints

worldview_premises.premise: Each market has a trend lookback that falls in the mean-reversion zone of its adjustment process, which depends on its physical nature, especially in commodities; markets are already traded at different speeds because costly-to-trade markets use slower signals.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning; no test shown

worldview_premises.premise: A 5x valuation multiplier in an inflationary asset process would spill over to bonds through rebalancing and show up as a positive bond-equity correlation, which has appeared in the last two years as a warning sign.
worldview_premises.support: Rebalancing logic; observation of correlation

worldview_premises.premise: Rising inflation from a low level is good for equities and from above-median inflation is bad; bonds always lose when inflation rises because yields rise; commodity trend and fixed-income trend both do well in inflationary periods in the Man paper's backtest to 1925.
worldview_premises.support: Man AHL paper by Otto Van Hemert (May 2021), which predicted 2022 behaviour

worldview_premises.premise: Trend returns depend on the share of markets trending: it breaks even at about a 40% hit ratio, the last couple of years had about 30% and 2021-22 about 60%, so the strategy bleeds like an option purchase and then pays when many markets trend.
worldview_premises.support: Own experience as a manager; no table shown

worldview_premises.premise: Long-only commodities have negative carry (storage and financing) and large losses in other periods, so trend gives inflation protection with lower downside; inflation changes slowly, matching the speed of trend, while equity crises can happen in two days and only give a second-response hedge.
worldview_premises.support: Cost-of-carry argument; no data in the call

worldview_premises.premise: TIPS and long-dated bonds combine inflation and duration exposure which offset, and housing suffers from higher mortgage rates, so real assets do not reliably hedge inflation in an inflationary episode.
worldview_premises.support: Duration reasoning; 2022 experience (Alan adds REITs)

worldview_premises.premise: Investors with inflation-plus mandates rarely use CTAs, yet active strategies such as CTAs with commodity exposure benefit from inflation volatility, unlike TIPS or real estate.
worldview_premises.support: Conversations with sovereign wealth funds and pensions

worldview_premises.premise: Alternative-beta (QIS) products lose about 60% of their backtest Sharpe once live (a backtest Sharpe of 1 gives about 0.4), even for carry and trend; a 50% haircut on backtests is appropriate before allocating.
worldview_premises.support: Study of about 200 products by Barclays researchers (2017), found only after asking for it; own practice of 50% haircuts

worldview_premises.premise: In trend following the signal is a commodity worth about 0.2 Sharpe per market; value comes from portfolio construction, risk management and execution.
worldview_premises.support: Own judgment; the spiky return profile of a QIS trend index as evidence

decision_process.practice: Match trend speed to each market's adjustment dynamics (slower for commodities with year-long supply response, faster for equities), noting that liquidity already imposes slower speeds on costly markets.
decision_process.why: A lookback in the mean-reversion zone of a market loses money

decision_process.practice: Prefer evidence that works out of sample and apply a 50% haircut to backtests before allocating to a new strategy.
decision_process.why: QIS data show about a 60% Sharpe haircut

decision_process.practice: Spend effort on portfolio construction, risk management and execution rather than a better signal.
decision_process.why: Signals are widely known and worth about 0.2 Sharpe per market

decision_process.practice: Use commodity-heavy trend (not long-only commodities or TIPS) for inflation protection; hold through low hit-ratio periods because breakeven is about 40% of markets trending.
decision_process.why: Bleeds slowly, then pays when many markets trend

decision_process.practice: Trade illiquid, niche markets with only about 25% correlation to the liquid trend universe, so peers' QIS products are not direct competitors.

speakers.evidence_style: Reads academic papers and critiques their identification; back-of-envelope calculations, market micro-structure examples and his own manager experience; prefers out-of-sample evidence and admits he is a pessimist about performance.

current_views.view: Fixed-income trend is very difficult: prices go up and down in a choppy range and the UK kept rates at 4%.
A positive bond-equity correlation seen over the last two years is a warning sign that equities may be in an inflationary asset process.
current_views.reasoning: Rebalancing spillover from equities to bonds.

current_views.view: There is a bit of a bubble in the equity market, but the 5x multiplier is probably nearer one; if flows reverse the downturn could be a roller coaster.
current_views.reasoning: Reverse causality critique; amplification if multiplier is real.

current_views.view: If interest rates stay put and inflation picks up from a low level, equities are not too bad and commodity and fixed-income trend should do well.
Trend followers should trust and improve the process through low hit-ratio periods (about 30% in the last couple of years).

worldview_premises.premise: QE works partly through a portfolio-transmission channel from safe bonds into riskier bonds and then risky assets; a large equity multiplier would caution central banks about QE.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Corrected claim: the 0.25-0.75 figure for fixed income is a price-impact multiplier (versus 5 for equities), not an economist's elasticity; the speaker uses 'elasticity' loosely for both.

Garbled number: CTA-driven quarterly flows are given as 'about 0.2% 2%' of market value; calling it 'not far from the 6%' fits 2% better than 0.2%, so the size of the reverse-causality effect is uncertain.
The claim that the multiplier is 'a little above one' is asserted from a back-of-envelope; there is no re-estimation, and the paper's authors use an instrument designed to isolate flows.
Positive stock-bond correlation is offered as a warning of an equity inflationary process, but an inflation regime also raises the correlation; no test separates the two explanations.
Hit-ratio figures (40% breakeven, 30% recent, 60% in 2021-22) are unsourced.
Man AHL's 25% annualised in high inflation comes from a backtest back to 1925 (earlier data may be less tradable); the out-of-sample match is 2021-22 only, one episode.
The 60% Sharpe haircut comes from a 2017 study with data to about 2015, reached through a personal favour; it is not recent and may not describe present QIS trend products.
Commercial interest: Yoav runs a CTA and argues that CTAs add value over QIS products and that signals are a commodity; he admits QIS offers low fees, customisation and capital efficiency.

The statement that bonds 'always' lose when inflation rises holds as a directional claim but the speaker also says equities depend on the starting inflation level; no thresholds are quantified beyond 'above median'.

Alan's description of equities as Giffen goods is a loose use of the term (a Giffen good is a specific case of upward-sloping demand) and is presented as known in the literature, not as a result of the paper.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs said to matter: any pick-up in inflation (delayed US data after the shutdown), the rate path (peak reached, easing), the sign of the stock-bond correlation (positive as a warning), the share of markets trending (hit ratio above 40%), flows into equities and trend-following flows, and fixed-income range-bound behaviour. Horizons are quarterly for the flow multiplier, a year for commodity adjustment and the next inflation episode for trend.
reader_inferences: (reader) The framework suggests a testable rule: trend lookback should scale with the physical adjustment time of each market (about a year for commodities, a week for equity ETFs), which can be tested by market.
(reader) The reverse-causality critique implies the inelastic-markets multiplier includes a trend component; it could be tested by controlling for lagged returns.
(reader) The 60% haircut implies a backtest-to-live shrinkage factor of about 0.4 that could be used as a prior when judging any new strategy, including candidate screens in this project.
(reader) The hit-ratio statistic is a useful regime variable for trend: breakeven near 40% of markets trending, 30% recently, 60% in 2021-22.
